title: Impact of Antiepileptic Drug Use on Second-Trimester Screening Test Parameters in Pregnancy
content: Background/Objectives: Use of antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) during pregnancy is critical for seizure control in women with epilepsy but raises concerns regarding the use of these drugs and their possible effect on maternal serum biochemical markers used for second-trimester prenatal screening. The aim of this study was to assess the effect of AEDs on maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), unconjugated estriol (uE3), and human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) during serum biomarker analysis in second-trimester prenatal screening. Methods: This retrospective cohort study included 43 pregnant women using AEDs (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, carbamazepine, or combined therapy) and 43 matched controls without medication use. Groups were matched based on maternal age, gravidity, parity, abortion history, gestational age at testing, body mass index, and smoking status using propensity score matching. Serum AFP, uE3, and hCG levels measured between 15–20 weeks of gestation were compared between groups. Results: Pregnant women taking AEDs had significantly higher maternal serum AFP (1.34 ± 0.42 vs. 1.01 ± 0.31 MoM; p <  0.001) and uE3 (1.28 ± 0.39 vs. 1.05 ± 0.34 MoM; p = 0.004) compared to controls. However, hCG did not differ significantly between groups (1.07 ± 0.46 vs. 1.01 ± 0.42 MoM; p = 0.523). Regarding the AED subgroup (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, or carbamazepine), there were no significant differences in serum biomarkers (p  > 0.05). Conclusions: The use of AEDs during pregnancy significantly alters second-trimester maternal serum biochemical markers, including our primary concerns, AFP and uE3, which could cause inaccurate interpretations of second-trimester prenatal screening. Clinicians should carefully consider maternal medication exposure when interpreting these biochemical markers in pregnant women with epilepsy to prevent misclassification of fetal risks and avoid unnecessary invasive procedures.
